terms.plain: Recording revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, rather than when cash moves. Gives a truer picture of a period, at the price of judgement.
terms.formal: The recognition of economic events in the period in which they occur, independent of the timing of associated cash flows.

terms.plain: A snapshot of what a company owns and owes at one instant. Assets equal liabilities plus equity, always, by construction.
terms.formal: A statement of financial position at a point in time, presenting assets, liabilities and equity such that assets equal the sum of the other two.

terms.plain: Cash spent on long-lived assets. Maintenance capex replaces what wore out and cannot be stopped for long; growth capex adds capacity and can.
terms.formal: Cash outflows for the acquisition or improvement of property, plant, equipment and other long-lived assets, reported within investing activities.

terms.plain: How many days a company's cash is tied up between paying for something and being paid for it. Days sales outstanding plus days inventory, minus days payable.
terms.formal: DSO + DIO − DPO, expressed in days; a negative cycle indicates the business is financed by its customers and suppliers.

terms.plain: The statement showing where cash actually came from and went, split into operating, investing and financing. The one to read first.
terms.formal: A statement reconciling opening and closing cash balances through operating, investing and financing activities over a period.

terms.plain: Current assets divided by current liabilities — a rough test of whether short-term obligations are covered by short-term resources.
terms.formal: Current assets divided by current liabilities; the quick ratio excludes inventory from the numerator.

terms.plain: The accountant's estimate of how much of a long-lived asset was used up this period. Not a cash payment now, and a real cost — the asset needs replacing.
terms.formal: The systematic allocation of the cost of a tangible asset over its estimated useful life; amortisation is the equivalent for intangibles.

terms.plain: How long stock sits before it is sold, in days. Measured against cost of goods sold rather than revenue, because inventory is carried at cost.
terms.formal: Inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by the number of days in the period.

terms.plain: How long the company takes to pay its own suppliers, in days. Effectively free financing — and stretching it has a relationship cost.
terms.formal: Accounts payable divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by the number of days in the period.

terms.plain: How long customers take to pay, in days. Receivables divided by revenue, times 365. Rising DSO with flat revenue is an early warning.
terms.formal: Accounts receivable divided by revenue, multiplied by the number of days in the period.

terms.plain: Earnings before interest and taxes — operating profit after the cost of assets wearing out, but before financing and tax. Stricter than EBITDA.
terms.formal: Operating profit after depreciation and amortisation and before interest expense and income taxes.

terms.plain: Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation. A rough proxy for the cash a business generates before financing and accounting choices.
terms.formal: Operating earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation. Widely used in leveraged transactions as a comparable earnings measure, though it excludes real cash costs including capital expenditure.

terms.plain: Selling receivables to a third party for cash now, at a discount. Improves reported collection days and operating cash flow, and is financing rather than efficiency.
terms.formal: The sale or assignment of trade receivables to a financier at a discount, transferring collection and sometimes credit risk.

terms.plain: The cash left after running the business and maintaining its assets — the money actually available to service debt or reach an owner.
terms.formal: Operating cash flow less capital expenditure; variants differ in whether interest has been deducted, so specify whether the measure is to the firm or to equity.

terms.plain: The statement showing revenue down to profit for a period. Built on accruals, so it records revenue when earned rather than when the cash arrives.
terms.formal: A statement of financial performance over a reporting period, presenting revenue, expenses and resulting profit or loss on an accrual basis.

terms.plain: Operating earnings divided by the interest bill. The ratio with a deadline attached: can the company pay its lenders out of what it earns?
terms.formal: EBIT or EBITDA divided by interest expense; the EBIT version is stricter because it accounts for the consumption of assets.

terms.plain: Gross borrowings less cash, on the logic that cash could repay debt tomorrow. Only net the cash that can actually reach the borrowing entity.
terms.formal: Total interest-bearing liabilities less cash and cash equivalents; analytically, restricted or trapped cash should be excluded from the offset.

terms.plain: How much of reported profit is recurring, cash-backed and genuinely attributable to the business. In private deals, a separate diligence workstream.
terms.formal: An assessment of the sustainability, cash conversion and attribution of reported earnings, including the basis of any presented adjustments.

terms.plain: Accumulated profits that have not been paid out as dividends. This is where each year's net income lands on the balance sheet.
terms.formal: The cumulative net income of an entity less cumulative distributions to owners, reported within equity.

terms.plain: The cash tied up in day-to-day operations: receivables plus inventory less payables. Remember the direction — working capital going up means cash going out.
terms.formal: Current operating assets less current operating liabilities; the change in the balance is a cash flow item within operating activities.
